# Brakes go to floor after bleeding

A brake pedal that drops to the floor immediately upon engine startup, while remaining firm when the engine is off, points directly to a vacuum leak in the hydraulic circuit or the booster itself. In your specific case involving a 1997 Honda Civic with front disc and rear drum brakes, the symptoms you are describingâa firm pedal with the engine off but a collapsed pedal with the engine runningâindicate that the engine's vacuum is being used to push fluid back into the master cylinder rather than helping move it forward.

When the engine is off, the hydraulic system relies solely on the mechanical force applied by your foot against the friction of the brake pads and shoes. Since you recently replaced both rear wheel cylinders and front calipers, and ensured no air was visible during the bleeding process, the fluid path appears physically intact. However, once the engine starts, the vacuum assist modulator inside the booster engages. This component uses engine intake vacuum to create a pressure differential that multiplies your foot force. If this seal fails or if there is an internal leak within the master cylinder bore, the vacuum draws brake fluid backward through the wheel cylinders and calipers instead of providing assist.

The fact that you are seeing fluid return to the reservoir confirms this mechanism is active but failing in reverse. You mentioned replacing the master cylinder three years ago and recently installing a new unit from NAPA. Even with a fresh unit, manufacturing defects or incorrect bench bleeding can lead to premature failure. If the internal seals in the new master cylinder are not seating perfectly against the bore walls, the vacuum created by the engine will pull fluid past these seals and out through your wheel cylinders. This is often mistaken for a leak at the wheels, but the source is actually upstream.

To diagnose this, you need to verify the integrity of the booster and the master cylinder interface. A common pitfall after a major rebuild like yours is assuming that because the pedal feels firm with the engine off, the hydraulic system is completely sealed. It is not; the booster relies on an air-tight seal between the pushrod and the master cylinder piston. If that seal is compromised, or if the vacuum diaphragm inside the booster is torn, the system loses its assist function immediately.

Given the age of the vehicle and the recent failure of components under high pressure (the exploding drum cylinder), it is highly probable that the vacuum hose connecting the intake manifold to the booster has degraded internally. These rubber hoses are notorious for developing micro-cracks that allow air into the system, disrupting the vacuum assist. Check the condition of this hose; if it feels spongy or shows signs of drying out, replace it before condemning the master cylinder.

If the vacuum line is intact and the new master cylinder still leaks fluid to the reservoir under engine load, the unit itself is likely defective. In this scenario, replacing the booster assembly or rebuilding the master cylinder with a high-quality seal kit from a reputable source is necessary. Do not overlook the possibility of air trapped in the booster reservoir port if the bleeder screw was left open too long during installation, though your description of fluid pouring out suggests a more significant internal failure.

Before returning to the shop, perform a simple test: disconnect the vacuum hose from the top of the booster with the engine running. If the pedal immediately becomes hard and stops leaking into the reservoir, the issue is isolated to the booster or its vacuum line. If the leak persists, the master cylinder bore is likely scored or the internal seals are blown, requiring replacement of that component as well.
